ios.desc:
Contadino helps you turn intention into momentum. Built around the Pomodoro technique, Contadino is a beautifully designed focus tracker that helps you work with clarity, build better habits, and see your progress grow over time without turning your brain into a spreadsheet.

Whether you are coding, writing, studying, or tackling the never-ending life admin pile, Contadino keeps you gently on track and quietly honest about where your time really goes.

What Contadino does best:
- Stay focused, one session at a time. Break your work into focused intervals and restorative breaks. Each session is logged automatically so you can build a rhythm that actually sticks.
- See distractions, not just results. Track completed and interrupted sessions to understand where your focus drifts and where it thrives.
- Understand your productivity. Explore clear, thoughtful stats across days, weeks, months, and years. Patterns emerge and habits become visible.
- Make it yours. Choose from multiple beautifully crafted themes and adjust session and break lengths to fit how you actually work.
- Works everywhere you do. Contadino syncs across iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, so your focus follows you.
- Private by design. Your data lives on your devices and in iCloud, never sold, never shared.

Contadino does not try to make you a productivity superhero. It just helps you show up, again and again, with a little more intention than yesterday.

quotes.text:
This is very similar to my flow.  I start a 25 minute timer, and work for at least that amount of time, if I get interrupted during that first 25 minutes I count that as an interruption (which I tally).  From there I count the number of 25 minute blocks I work, which include any rolling timers (25 minute blocks after the first 25 minutes).

I did this on paper for a few months and eventually turned it into an app called Contadino for macOS, iOS, watchOS, and visionOS (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/contadino/id1672167389).
quotes.story_title: Ask HN: Alternatives to the Pomodoro technique?
